R0036.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) Bypass
R0036.definition: Cracking or bypassing multi-factor authentication factors during the identity verification process, directly obtaining authenticated session access.
R0036.description:
Obtaining MFA verification factors through brute force enumeration — such as cracking SMS verification codes, last digits of ID numbers, email verification codes, or OTP tokens; or exploiting flaws in the authentication process — such as forging trusted device fingerprints or requesting non-MFA login pages — to bypass MFA verification.

As attack techniques evolve, MFA is no longer an insurmountable barrier. Key attack paths also include: ① AiTM adversary-in-the-middle attacks: intercepting authentication flows through reverse proxies to steal post-MFA session cookies; ② MFA fatigue attacks (R0036-001): pushing massive MFA verification requests to targets, forcing users to accidentally confirm due to fatigue; ③ SIM swapping: using social engineering to transfer victim phone numbers to attacker-controlled SIM cards to receive SMS verification codes; ④ Session token theft: stealing session cookies stored in browsers through infostealers; ⑤ MFA credential phishing: collecting both passwords and real-time 2FA tokens through phishing pages simultaneously. According to the CrowdStrike 2026 Global Threat Report, 82% of cyber attacks use no malware but instead bypass MFA through identity and session token theft.
R0036.influence: Will bypass existing MFA multi-factor authentication mechanisms, leading to account compromise; directly causes account security defenses to be breached, enterprise core systems and data can be accessed without authorization, and traditional MFA protection becomes ineffective.

observables: The MFA verification endpoint is hit at high frequency, with a single account trying different verification codes multiple times within a short window
The login flow shows requests to non-MFA login pages, or device fingerprints are forged as trusted devices
After MFA verification passes, the session is immediately used for sensitive operations, inconsistent with normal user behavior timing
Session cookies are obtained immediately after authentication, with the login state bypassing MFA and being directly reused
User devices show infostealer characteristics, with browser session cookies being exfiltrated
The MFA verification flow is intercepted by a man-in-the-middle proxy, with session tokens generated on anomalous nodes

R0036-001.title: MFA Fatigue Attack
R0036-001.definition: MFA fatigue attack refers to hackers repeatedly sending push notification approval requests after obtaining login credentials, tricking users into granting account access. Eventually, users approve the notification out of fatigue or inattention.
R0036-001.description: The hacker continuously triggers login approval request push notifications to the victim's device. The victim is initially confused and has about 30% trust. The attacker then uses social engineering to contact the victim, posing as an IT administrator and claiming the system has a problem that requires approving the notification to stop the pushes. The victim's trust rises to about 80% because they believe a real IT admin would know about the issue so quickly and know their name and department. Many employees then comply with the 'fake admin's' instructions.
R0036-001.influence: Will bypass existing MFA multi-factor authentication mechanisms, leading to account compromise.

references.title: Nearly 1,000 Data Breaches in Q1 2023, Affecting 1,204 Companies Across 38 Industries

observables: A large volume of MFA approval requests is pushed to the same account within a short window, far exceeding normal login frequency
The originating IP/location of MFA push requests does not match the user's historical login profile
The request the user ultimately approves originates from an anomalous device or a foreign location, with sensitive operations immediately following approval
